t:
Section 605(a) (20 U.S.C. 1125(a)) is amended—
    (1) in paragraph (8), by striking “and” after the semicolon; 
    (2) in paragraph (9), by striking the period and inserting a semicolon; and 
    (3) by adding at the end the following:“(10) evaluation of the extent to which programs assisted under this title reflect diverse perspectives and a wide range of views and generate debate on world regions and international affairs, as described in the grantee’s application;“(11) the systematic collection, analysis, and dissemination of data that contribute to achieving the purposes of this part; and“(12) support for programs or activities to make data collected, analyzed, or disseminated under this section publicly available and easy to understand.”.

fable.w: This section only adds authorized research, evaluation, and data-dissemination activities to an existing grant program. The tempting reading is that "diverse perspectives," "generate debate," and making data "publicly available" signal public involvement, but these describe the content of grant-funded programs and the release of data, not consultation with outside parties before a federal decision. The reference to a grantee's application is a grant application, which the definition expressly excludes.
fable.s: evaluation of the extent to which programs assisted under this title reflect diverse perspectives and a wide range of views and generate debate on world regions and international affairs, as described in the grantee’s application

qwen_block.w: This section amends the criteria for evaluating grant programs. It requires the evaluation of whether programs reflect diverse perspectives as described in the grantee's application. This is an internal assessment of grant compliance and quality, not a requirement for the federal government to consult with outside parties, hold public hearings, or seek public comment before making a decision. The 'diverse perspectives' mentioned are part of the program content, not the decision-making process involving external stakeholders.
qwen_block.s: (10) evaluation of the extent to which programs assisted under this title reflect diverse perspectives and a wide range of views and generate debate on world regions and international affairs, as described in the grantee’s application;
qwen_block.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "evaluation of the extent to which programs... reflect diverse perspectives" implies a process of gathering input from the public or outside experts. However, the text describes criteria for evaluating grant programs based on the "grantee's application" and internal data collection. It does not mandate a public comment period, a hearing, or consultation with outside parties before a decision is made. The "diverse perspectives" refer to the content of the educational programs, not the decision-making process itself. Furthermore, the section is primarily an amendment to a list of evaluation criteria for grants, which falls under the "applications for benefits or grants" exclusion if interpreted as part of the application process, or simply as internal agency evaluation criteria. There is no requirement for the federal government to consult with outsiders.

opus.w: The amendment only adds evaluation, data-collection, and data-dissemination activities to a list of things the program can fund. Making data public sends information outward. It does not require any consultation, comment period, hearing, or advisory body with outside parties before a federal decision. The mentions of 'debate' and the 'grantee's application' describe how funded programs work and the grant process, and grant applications are expressly excluded from participation.
opus.s: (12) support for programs or activities to make data collected, analyzed, or disseminated under this section publicly available and easy to understand.
opus.b: 1. **Thinking it through.** This amendment adds three activities to a list of things that can be funded: evaluating whether programs "reflect diverse perspectives" and "generate debate," collecting and analyzing data, and making that data public. The tempting reading is that "generate debate," "publicly available," and "the grantee's application" mean outsiders are involved. That reading fails. "Debate" describes what the funded programs should produce, not a way for the public to weigh in on a federal decision. Publishing data sends information out to the public; it doesn't bring the public into a decision. A grant application is excluded by the definition.

qwen_chat.w: This section lists criteria for evaluating programs or grants, specifically regarding whether they reflect diverse perspectives. It does not require the federal government to consult with outside parties before making a decision. The mention of 'diverse perspectives' refers to the content of the programs, not a participatory process involving external stakeholders in the decision-making itself.
qwen_chat.s: (10) evaluation of the extent to which programs assisted under this title reflect diverse perspectives and a wide range of views and generate debate on world regions and international affairs, as described in the grantee’s application;
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "evaluation of the extent to which programs... reflect diverse perspectives" implies consulting with diverse groups. However, the text describes criteria for evaluating grants or programs, not a process for the government to consult with outsiders before making a decision. The "diverse perspectives" are part of the program content, not a participatory mechanism for decision-making.
